COMPTROLLER’S DECISION

This decision is considered final on February 5, 2024_, unless a motion for rehearing is timely filed; this date of finality is calculated based on the Administrative Procedure Act (APA).[1] The failure to timely file a motion for rehearing may result in adverse legal consequences.

Administrative Law Judge (ALJ) Kimberly LaFlair of the State Office of Administrative Hearings (SOAH) issued a Proposal for Decision (PFD) that includes Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law. SOAH served the PFD on each party and each party was given an opportunity to file exceptions and replies with SOAH in accordance with SOAH’s rules of procedure. The ALJ recommended that the Comptroller adopt the PFD as written.

After review and consideration, IT IS ORDERED that the PFD is adopted as written.

The result from this Decision is Attachment A. The ALJ’s recommendation letter is Attachment B. The PFD as written is Attachment C. Attachments A, B, and C are incorporated by reference.

Attachment A reflects a liability.[2]

The total sum of the tax, penalty, and interest is due and payable 20 days after a comptroller’s decision becomes final.[3] If such sum is not timely paid, an additional penalty of 10 percent of the taxes due will accrue.

TEXAS COMPTROLLER OF PUBLIC ACCOUNTS

BEFORE THE STATE OFFICE OF ADMINISTRATIVE HEARINGS

Proposal for Decision

************** (Petitioner) was audited by the Tax Division (Staff) of the Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts (Comptroller) for sales and use tax compliance and a liability consisting of tax, penalty, and accrued interest was assessed. Petitioner requested redetermination of the assessment, contending the audit was based on incorrect hours of operation and incorrectly assumed perfect sales conditions. Petitioner also contends the audit failed to fully account for the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on sales. Staff argues Petitioner’s evidence is insufficient to support his contentions. In this Proposal for Decision, the Administrative Law Judge (ALJ) recommends that the assessment be upheld.

I. NOTICE, JURISDICTION, AND PROCEDURAL HISTORY

Staff referred this case to the State Office of Administrative Hearings (SOAH) and, on August 28, 2023, issued a Notice of Hearing by Written Submission. On September 15, 2023, ALJ Kimberly LaFlair issued an order setting the written submission hearing. Preston Tom represented Staff, and Petitioner was represented by **************. The contested case record closed November 20, 2023.

There are no issues of notice or jurisdiction; therefore, those matters are set out in the Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law without further discussion.

II. REASONS FOR DECISION

A. EVIDENCE

Petitioner did not submit exhibits in the written submission hearing.

Staff submitted the pleadings exchanged between the parties prior to referring the matter to SOAH and offered the following exhibits:

1. Hearing Request Receipt;

2. Texas Notification of Audit Results;

3. Penalty and Interest Waiver Worksheet;

4. Audit Report; and

5. Audit Plan.

6. Staff’s exhibits are admitted without objection.

B. AGREED ADJUSTMENTS

There are no agreed adjustments.

C. MATERIAL FACTS AND ISSUES PRESENTED

Petitioner operated two food trucks that sold Honduran food. Outlet 1 is located at ADDRESS, CITY, Texas. Outlet 2 operated at two separate locations and closed in May 2021. Staff initiated a sales and use tax audit in September 2021 for the period of April 1, 2017, through December 31, 2020.

Petitioner did not charge sales tax separately but contends he included tax in the total sales price of his food. Petitioner did not keep any sales or purchase invoices, and he kept track of his sales in a handwritten notebook with the date and the price of the sale. Only cash was accepted for purchases and Petitioner did not maintain a bank account. Petitioner did not have a cash register and did not provide receipts for customer purchases.

Petitioner provided federal income tax returns for 2017, 2018, and 2019. The sales on the Schedule C attached to the returns matched Petitioner’s sales reported for 2017 and 2018. No sales were reported for the business in 2019.

Because Petitioner did not keep records, the auditor, along with her supervisor, conducted an observation and headcount for Outlet 1 as Outlet 2 closed on May 1, 2021. They observed approximately 27 different dishes on the menu, with the most popular item being the baleadas.[4] Prices were not included on the menu, but they ordered three baleadas and were charged $12. Only cash was accepted, and they did not receive a receipt for the order. Sales were observed for three hours, from 12:45 p.m. to 3:45 p.m.

The auditor totaled the observed sales transactions, calculated an hourly average, and then used that value to estimate taxable sales (i.e., multiplying the hourly value by the estimated food truck operational hours). Petitioner’s reported taxable sales were subtracted from the net estimated taxable sales and the remaining amounts were scheduled as additional taxable sales. The auditor performed a similar estimation for Outlet 2, but only for the periods of January 2019, February 2019, and April 2020 based on information provided by Petitioner that the food truck at that location was not in working order for many months.

During a conference with the auditor, Petitioner claimed that the hours listed on the Outlet 1 truck are not the actual hours the food truck operated. Petitioner also claimed the food truck did not open every day. The auditor decided to use eight hours per day and five days per week for the estimation. Due to the Covid-19 pandemic, the auditor reduced the open hours for the first and second quarter in 2020. The auditor decided that due to the minimal number of estimated sales for the second food truck, she would not assess Outlet 2. The additional taxable sales were updated based on the foregoing information.

The auditor again met with Petitioner, and he claimed that the baleadas only sold for $1.50 to $2.00 when he first opened the business, which was 50% of the current pricing. Petitioner also claimed that when the business first opened it was open for fewer hours. The auditor agreed to change the business days open from 5 days to 4 days for 2017 and 2018. The food price for those years was also lowered by 50% and an updated assessment for additional taxable sales was provided to Petitioner.

On February 28, 2022, Staff issued an audit report and Texas Notification of Audit Results to Petitioner. The assessment included tax, 10% late filing penalty, and accrued interest. Petitioner timely requested redetermination.

Petitioner did not provide any additional information or evidence during redetermination or during the hearings process to support any adjustments to the assessment. Staff did not agree to adjust the assessment and referred the matter to SOAH.

D. ANALYSIS AND RECOMMENDATION

Texas imposes a tax on each sale of a taxable item in this state. Tex. Tax Code § 151.051. The term “taxable item” includes tangible personal property and taxable services. Id. § 151.010. All sellers and all other persons storing, using, or consuming in this state a taxable item purchased from a retailer shall keep records in the form the Comptroller requires. Tex. Tax Code § 151.025(a); 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.281(a)(1). For example, a seller must keep records of all gross receipts, including documentation in the form of receipts from each sale occurring during each reporting period. Tex. Tax Code § 151.025(a)(1). In addition, a seller’s records must substantiate any claimed deductions or exclusions authorized by law. Id. § 151.025(a)(3); 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.281(b). If a taxpayer fails to keep accurate records of gross receipts, gross purchases, deductions, and exclusions, the Comptroller may take actions that include estimating the person’s tax liability based on the best information available. Tex. Tax Code §§ 111.0042(d), .008(a).

Petitioner disagrees with the audit results and contends that the auditor did not correctly account for his business hours, incorrectly assumed perfect sales conditions for each day, and did not accurately account for the Covid-19 pandemic. Other than handwritten notes regarding sales, Petitioner did not provide any source records to support his contentions. A taxpayer cannot defeat an assessment based on the burden of proof by withholding or failing to provide documentation. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision Nos. 102,386 (2014), 105,892 (2012). Treating transactions that lack documentation as taxable is supported by statute. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision Nos. 103,035 (2014), 39,765 (2003). Additionally, the Comptroller has routinely held that summary documents that are created by the taxpayer and submitted without underlying support are tantamount to bare assertions, i.e., they are not considered evidence. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision Nos. 117,167, 117,168, and 117,169 (2023). Petitioner’s handwritten notes are not supported by any documentation or source records and are therefore not considered evidence.

The audit consisted of one exam, Exam 100, where adjustments were made for additional taxable sales, and which was estimated due to lack of records. The record evidence shows that the auditor considered Petitioner’s differing business days by reducing the operating days from 5 to 4 for 2017 and 2018. The auditor also reduced the additional taxable sales during the first two quarters of 2020 to account for the pandemic, and she did not assess transactions related to Outlet 2. Finally, the auditor decreased Petitioner’s additional taxable sales by only assessing 50% of the current price of Petitioner’s sales of baleadas for 2017 and 2018.

Staff contends Petitioner’s records were unreliable and incomplete and that the estimated audit is based on the best information available. The ALJ agrees, and Staff’s prima facie case to show the scheduled transactions were taxable is met. Petitioner’s evidence is insufficient to demonstrate, by a preponderance of evidence, that any items in dispute were scheduled erroneously. 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 1.26(e). Petitioner’s contentions should be denied, and the audit assessment should be upheld.

III. FINDINGS OF FACT

1. ************** (Petitioner) operated two food trucks that sold Honduran food.

2. Outlet 1 is located at ADDRESS, CITY, Texas. Outlet 2 operated at two separate locations and closed in May 2021.

3. The Tax Division (Staff) of the Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts (Comptroller) initiated a sales and use tax audit in September 2021 for the period of April 1, 2017, through December 31, 2020.

4. Petitioner did not charge sales tax separately but contends he included tax in the total sales price of his food.

5. Petitioner did not keep any sales or purchase invoices, and he kept track of his sales in a handwritten notebook with the date and the price of the sale.

6. Only cash was accepted for purchases and Petitioner did not maintain a bank account. Petitioner did not have a cash register and did not provide receipts for customer purchases.

7. Petitioner provided federal income tax returns for 2017, 2018, and 2019. The sales on the Schedule C attached to the returns matched Petitioner’s sales reported for 2017 and 2018. No sales were reported for the business in 2019.

8. The auditor and her supervisor conducted an observation and headcount for Outlet 1 as Outlet 2 closed on May 1, 2021. They observed approximately 27 different dishes on the menu, with the most popular item being the baleadas. Prices were not included on the menu, but they ordered three baleadas and were charged $12. Only cash was accepted, and they did not receive a receipt for the order. Sales were observed for three hours, from 12:45 p.m. to 3:45 p.m.

9. The auditor totaled the observed sales transactions, calculated an hourly average, and then used that value to estimate taxable sales (i.e., multiplying the hourly value by the estimated food truck operational hours).

10. Petitioner’s reported taxable sales were subtracted from the net estimated taxable sales and the remaining amounts were scheduled as additional taxable sales.

11. The auditor performed a similar estimation for Outlet 2, but only for the periods of January 2019, February 2019, and April 2020 based on information provided by Petitioner that the food truck was not in working order for many months.

12. Petitioner claimed that the hours listed on the Outlet 1 truck are not the actual hours the food truck operated. Petitioner also claimed the food truck did not open every day.

13. The auditor decided to use eight hours per day and five days per week for the estimation.

14. Due to the Covid-19 pandemic, the auditor reduced the open hours for the first and second quarter in 2020.

15. The auditor decided that due to the minimal number of estimated sales for the second food truck, she would not assess Outlet 2.

16. The auditor agreed to change the business days open from 5 days to 4 days for 2017 and 2018. The food price for those years was also lowered by 50% and an updated assessment for additional taxable sales was provided to Petitioner.

17. On February 28, 2022, Staff issued an audit report and Texas Notification of Audit Results to Petitioner. The assessment included tax, 10% late filing penalty, and accrued interest.

18. Petitioner timely requested redetermination.

19. Petitioner did not provide any additional information or evidence during redetermination or during the hearings process to support any adjustments to the assessment.

20. Staff did not agree to adjust the assessment and referred the matter to the State Office of Administrative Hearings (SOAH).

21. On August 28, 2023, Staff issued a Notice of Hearing by Written Submission. Each notice contained a statement of the nature of the hearing; a statement of the legal authority and jurisdiction under which the hearing was to be held; a reference to the particular sections of the statutes and rules involved; and a short, plain statement of the factual matters asserted, or an attachment that incorporated by reference the factual matters asserted in the complaint or petition filed with the state agency.

22. On September 15, 2023, ALJ Kimberly LaFlair issued an order setting the written submission hearing.

23. The contested case record closed on November 20, 2023.

IV. CONCLUSIONS OF LAW

1. The Comptroller has jurisdiction over this matter. See Tex. Tax Code ch. 111.

2. SOAH has jurisdiction over matters related to the hearing in this matter, including the authority to issue a proposal for decision with findings of fact and conclusions of law. See Tex. Gov’t Code ch. 2003.

3. Staff provided proper and timely notice of the hearing. See Tex. Gov’t Code ch. 2001; Tex. Tax Code § 111.009.

4. Texas imposes a tax on each sale of a taxable item in this state. Tex. Tax Code § 151.051.

5. The term “taxable item” includes tangible personal property and taxable services. Tex. Tax Code § 151.010.

6. All sellers and all other persons storing, using, or consuming in this state a taxable item purchased from a retailer shall keep records in the form the Comptroller requires. Tex. Tax Code § 151.025(a); 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.281(a)(1).

7. A seller must keep records of all gross receipts, including documentation in the form of receipts from each sale occurring during each reporting period. Tex. Tax Code § 151.025(a)(1).

8. A seller’s records must substantiate any claimed deductions or exclusions authorized by law. Tex. Tax Code § 151.025(a)(3); 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.281(b).

9. If a taxpayer fails to keep accurate records of gross receipts, gross purchases, deductions, and exclusions, the Comptroller may take actions that include estimating the person’s tax liability based on the best information available. Tex. Tax Code §§ 111.0042(d), .008(a).

10. A taxpayer cannot defeat an assessment based on the burden of proof by withholding or failing to provide documentation. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision Nos. 102,386 (2014), 105,892 (2012).

11. Treating transactions that lack documentation as taxable is supported by statute. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision Nos. 103,035 (2014), 39,765 (2003).

12. The Comptroller has routinely held that summary documents that are created by the taxpayer and submitted without underlying support are tantamount to bare assertions, i.e., they are not considered evidence. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision Nos. 117,167, 117,168, and 117,169 (2023).

13. The ALJ finds Staff’s prima facie case to show the transactions were taxable is met.

14. The ALJ finds that Petitioner’s records were unreliable and incomplete and that the estimated audit is based on the best information available.

15. The ALJ finds that Petitioner’s evidence is insufficient to demonstrate, by a preponderance of evidence, that any items in dispute were scheduled erroneously. 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 1.26(e).

16. Petitioner’s contentions should be denied, and the audit assessment should be upheld.

SIGNED December 15, 2023

KIMBERLY LA FLAIR

PRESIDING ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGE
